objections.claim_attacked: global-route overflow dropped from 3.8% to 0.6% via hotspot-local density screens and NDR relaxations, without changing71.5%)

object density screens (max 65%) inside the six channels will, by construction, reduce the cell density in those regions, which means the global utilization number cannot stay at 71.5% unless those cells are spread into previously under-utilized regions elsewhere. The chip-level utilization is a weighted average; if you tighten the worst six channels from 71.5% to ≤65%, you either lower the global number or you have to spread cells into slack regions that would also need to be reported. Keeping 71.5% globally while capping six channels at 65% is mechanically inconsistent unless the global figure was rounded or is reported post-spreading with a misleading identical.
objections.corrected_version: Either report the global utilization as having risen slightly to ~72-73% (cells channel regions into adjacent slack regions), or report the channel-local utilization dropping to ≤65% with the global number updated. The two cannot both be unchanged.

objections.claim_attacked: DRC violations dropped from ~214,000 to 340 in one route pass with unchanged utilization and only 2 repair iterations to 0
objections.objection: 214,000 → 340 in a single route pass is a 99.8% reduction without any placement spreading (ization unchanged) and without rerunning CTS or power. Three soft measures (local density screens, NDR relaxation in two mid-layers, two pin swaps) cannot plausibly explain that magnitude. NDR relaxation on two mid-layers at most gives the router 2-4x more tracks in those channels, but if the underlying congestion is cell-driven, more routing resources alone don't help; you need cells moved. Pin-swap on two macros changes feedthrough patterns but two macros out of ~100 cannot move enough nets to explain this. A realistic reduction from 214k to ~10k-30k in one pass is plausible; to 340 implies the placement actually changed substantially, contradicting the unchanged-utilization claim.
objections.corrected_version: Either (a) report the violation count after 2-3 repair iterations that include cell moves / partial placement resizing in the channel regions (and update the utilization to reflect it), or (b) report a more modest first-pass reduction (e.g., ~30k-50k remaining) and an honest number of repair5-10) with a clear story about what each iteration did. The 214k → 340 → 0 narrative either hides real placement changes or hides repeat repair attempts.

objections.claim_attacked: WNS degradation of −12 ps accepted and 'recovered later during incremental optimization'
objections.objection: −12 ps of WNS degradation after route, on a 28nm DSP block, is not a 'small' change — it represents meaningful degradation of the timing wall. The claim that it was 'recovered later during incremental optimization' is hand-waving: post-route incremental floorplan has limited ability to recover setup slack, especially on paths that go through the modified channels. The wires through the relaxed-NDR regions are longer/worse SI, not better, so the −12 ps likely reflects real wire delay that incremental sizing cannot fully recover. Also, 'recovered later' is temporally undefined — signoff is the next gate, not 'later.'
objections.corrected_version: Either report the WNS as having been recovered to within the original signoff margin by explicit ECO sizing on the degraded paths, with a count of cells resized, or as a permanent signoff margin loss that the team accepted. Do not say 'recovered later during incremental optimization' without naming when and how.

objections.claim_attacked: non-default routing rules relaxed for two mid-layer metals within the channel regions only
objections.objection: NDR relaxation is unusual as a congestion fix — NDRs are typically tightened (wider spacing, double-cut vias) for SI/EM relief, not loosened for routing capacity. If by 'relaxed' they mean reducing wire-width/spacing constraints on two mid-layer metals in the channels, this can give the router more tracks but introduces SI risk on long parallel runs in a congested region — exactly where coupling is worst. For a DSP block with likely high-switching nets this is a real SI/EM problem that the story completely ignores. Also, mid-layer metals at 28nm are typically the thinner, higher-R layers; routing the critical long-haul signals there when the channels are 2-4 gcol wide (likely spanning a few hundred microns total) is suboptimal but not catastrophic.
objections.corrected_version: Clarify whether 'relaxed' means spacing/widetrack loosening (in which case the story needs an SI/cross-talk check) or whether it means something else like non-preferred direction allowance. Either way, report the SI delta on nets in those channels.

objections.claim_attacked: macro placement frozen because top-level feedthroughs and power-grid stripe locations were already derived from it
objections.objection: The justification for not reworking the floorplan is plausible on the schedule side but technically weak: at 28nm, modifying macro positions by tens of microns locally (not a global rework) is feasible without invalidating top-level feedthroughs, because the top-level typically runs over the macro channels and has its own slack. Also, power-grid stripes at 28nm are typically on a regular pitch and don't depend on individual macro positions — they're driven by IR-drop, not by macro layout. The story uses 'frozen' as a reason but the technical reasoning needs to be more precise: was it physical IP boundary / IO escape constraints, or was it schedule pressure dressed up as a technical blocker?
objections.corrected_version: Either name the specific top-level constraints that prevent macro movement (e.g., 'IO escape pitch requires macros to remain within X um of their current positions,' or 'package substrate breakout forces the west-edge macros to remain stationary'), or acknowledge that the constraint was schedule-driven.

objections.claim_attacked: pin-swap on two macro instances moving high-fanout pins away from the most congested channel
objections.objection: Pin-swap on hard macros is generally not legal — hard macro pins are fixed by the IP vendor and the abutment/pin access layer. Pin-swap implies soft macros or the ability to flip a side, but if these are SRAMs or hard IP, the pins cannot be 'swapped.' Also, even if legal, moving high-fanout pins on two macros out of ~100 cannot materially change the congestion of a channel that has feedthroughs from many macros and the standard-cell logic. The contribution is real but small; presenting it as part of the solution stack implies more impact than mechanism allows.
objections.corrected_version: Clarify what kind of pin-swap (orientation flip vs pin-assignment change on a soft block), and quantify the net-rerouting impact (how many nets shifted off the congested channel). Two macros out of 100 with maybe 30-50 high-fanout pins each moves tens of nets, not the hundreds-to-thousands needed.

missing_from_story: No mention of hold-fixing impact after the changes — routing detours and NDR relaxation typically increase wire delay and length, which worsens hold. A real postmortem would have a hold-violation count before and after, and any hold-fix buffer additions.

No mention of SI/cross-talk delta in the modified channels. Relaxing NDRs and rerouting through the same congested region introduces coupling on long parallel runs. At 28nm this is a known closure problem and the absence is conspicuous.

No mention of antenna violations or via-count changes from rerouting. Rerouting through tighter regions with relaxed spacing frequently increases antenna violations because longer wires on fewer layers accumulate more area per net.

No mention of ECO timing delta per corner / per mode. The −12 ps WNS is reported as a single number; a real pre-tapeout story includes per-corner and per-mode WNS/TNS, especially since the changes were to congestion and routing layers which affect setup and hold differently across PVT.

No quantitative statement of what 'small' WNS degradation means in context of the signoff margin — was the −12 ps within the original signoff margin (and therefore truly recoverable) or did it eat into margin that was already thin?
most_defensible_part: The causal chain that local congestion in macro channels at the west edge caused ~214k DRC violations after detailed route is plausible and reflects a well-known failure mode at 28nm — global route often undercounts congestion that detailed route reveals, especially where macro pin density creates local hot spots.
overall_note: The narrative has the right shape but is too tidy on the numbers: the violation reduction (214k → 340 → 0) and the unchanged-utilization claim are mutually inconsistent given the actions described, and the −12 ps WNS 'recovered later' is hand-waving that a real postmortem would quantify. The author's instincts on which knobs to pull (local density screens, NDR, pin-swap) are correct, but the magnitudes don't add up without hidden placement changes or repair iterations that the story elides. Revise to honestly report either larger utilization movement or more modest first-pass DRC reduction, and add per-corner timing, hold, and SI deltas.
